archetype.name: Rebuilding (new staff, run-stopping but leaky)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff under Mike LaFleur working from a roster that has been bad most of the decade, with a veteran bridge quarterback, a sound run defense and a secondary that gives up big plays.

report.headline: A 3-5 record that matches the play: stout against the run, exposed through the air
report.take:
Arizona is roughly what its record says. The Cardinals are 3-5, the point differential implies 3.1 wins, and Wins Over Expected sits at -0.14. Luck didn't sink them and didn't lift them. In LaFleur's first year, Jacoby Brissett has started every game and the offense is middling: 19th in EPA per play, 13th in success rate, running slightly more than expected. History matters here. This franchise won 3 games last year and 4 in each of 2022 and 2023, so a team that competes in some games without threatening is a step, not a slide.

The defense comes in two halves. Against the run it is good: ninth in rush EPA allowed, seventh by the play-by-play split, and fifth in missed-tackle rate. Against the pass it is close to the bottom of the league: 31st in pass EPA allowed, 30th in explosive pass rate, and 30th in EPA allowed to both WR1s and WR2s. Teams have stopped bothering with the ground game against Arizona and gone over the top. That is why the Cardinals rank last in points allowed even though their run defense is above average.

The offense is steadier than the scores look, but it has limits. The line wins on short yardage, converting 83.3% (4th), and keeps sacks down at a 5% rate (10th). It loses the ordinary run downs, though: backs average 2.07 yards before contact (29th) and the stuff rate ranks 25th. The passing game runs mostly through two players, Trey McBride with 86 targets and Michael Wilson with 81. That concentration now looks fragile. Kendrick Bourne is done for the year, Wilson broke two ribs at Dallas, and both Jeremiyah Love and Bam Knight came out of that game hurt.

The wins have come against offenses that rank 32nd and 10th today, and in a Dallas shootout against the league's worst defense. The losses to Detroit, Denver and Seattle were not close. Special teams at -1.79 EPA a game (26th) quietly cost points most weeks. The back half of the schedule is softer, with Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Washington all carrying losing records. A handful more wins is realistic. A playoff push is not.

strengths.title: A run defense that tackles
strengths.body: Arizona's front stops the run efficiently and finishes plays, with a missed-tackle rate among the league's lowest. That is a repeatable, scheme-and-personnel trait rather than a fluke of opponents. It will be tested with DT Walter Nolen out.

strengths.title: Ball control and short-yardage muscle
strengths.body: The offense stays on schedule well enough to rank sixth in time of possession. The line converts short-yardage downs at an elite clip, which keeps drives alive and shortens games, a sensible approach for a team whose secondary needs protecting. Sacks are also kept in check despite pressure numbers that are only middling.

strengths.title: McBride as the reliable hub
strengths.body: McBride leads the team in targets and gives Brissett a dependable middle-of-the-field option. With Bourne lost for the season and Wilson playing through broken ribs, his share should only grow. That makes him the offense's most bankable piece, and also its most obvious key for opponents to take away.

concerns.title: Secondary bleeding explosive plays
concerns.body: This is the defining flaw, not a sample-size quirk. Arizona is near the bottom in pass EPA allowed and explosive pass rate, and outside receivers have feasted. The pass rush ranks only 24th in pressure rate, so coverage is left exposed too long. There is no sign of a fix on the roster, so this should persist.

concerns.title: Run blocking that loses early downs
concerns.body: Backs are being hit almost at the line, and that caps the run game outside of short yardage. The 202-yard day at Dallas came against the league's worst defense, so it doesn't change the picture. Guard Jon Gaines is out and tackle Jayden Williams is questionable, which makes this harder to fix in the short term.

concerns.title: Thinning skill-position group
concerns.body: Bourne's season-ending fracture removes the third target. Wilson's broken ribs, Love's new ankle injury and Knight's concussion leave the offense leaning on McBride, Tyler Allgeier and depth players. Some of this is short-term, but the receiver room won't be whole again this year.

trend.note: Wins and blowout losses have alternated with no clear arc. A road win over Los Angeles as a 12.5-point underdog and an overtime shootout win at Dallas sit next to 24-point losses to Seattle and Detroit. The defense has given up 30 or more in five of the last six games.

nextGame.headline: Brissett's banged-up offense meets Seattle's top-two defense on the road
nextGame.body:
Seattle is built the opposite way from Arizona. The Seahawks have an elite defense, second in EPA allowed and third in pressure rate, and they allow almost nothing deep. Their offense ranks 25th in EPA and runs the ball despite a ground game that rates 29th. The Week 2 meeting in Arizona was ugly: the Cardinals managed 95 passing yards and lost 31-7. The Book has Seattle by 11.5 with a 44.5 total. Arizona's realistic plan is to shorten the game, stuff the Seahawks' weak run game and take what Seattle's 22nd-ranked short-pass defense gives underneath.

Availability cuts both ways. Arizona is without guard Jon Gaines, DT Walter Nolen and WR Kendrick Bourne. Michael Wilson (broken ribs), Jeremiyah Love (ankle), Bam Knight (concussion) and tackle Jayden Williams are all questionable, so Brissett could be working with McBride and very little else. Seattle came out of Monday's game with OT Charles Cross, a near every-snap starter, plus LB Uchenna Nwosu and WR Rashid Shaheed all inactive, and DT Leonard Williams nursing a stinger. Sam Darnold has started the last two games with Drew Lock out. If Cross can't go, a line that already ranks last in pressure allowed gets worse.

waysToWin.title: Collapse the pocket on Darnold
waysToWin.body: Seattle's line allows pressure more often than any in the league, and it may be missing Cross. Arizona's pressure rate is mediocre, but it converts pressure into sacks at the eighth-best rate. A few drive-killing sacks would stall an offense that already struggles to sustain drives.

waysToWin.title: Make Seattle run, and stop it
waysToWin.body: Seattle leans run-heavy anyway and its rushing EPA is among the league's worst, while Arizona's run defense is a genuine strength. Winning early downs keeps the Seahawks in third-and-long and keeps the ball away from the Cardinals' secondary. Arizona then has to cash in red-zone trips against a Seattle defense that ranks 29th in red-zone TD rate.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle
waysToWin.body: Seattle has been loose with the ball, with a turnover margin near the bottom of the league. A short field or two is the likeliest way for a limited Arizona offense to score against this defense.

waysToLose.title: Seattle's rush overwhelms a patched line
waysToLose.body: Without Gaines and possibly Williams, Arizona's front faces one of the league's best pressure units. In Week 2 that matchup produced negative passing and rushing EPA alike. If Brissett can't get the ball out to McBride on time, the offense stalls before Arizona's run defense can matter.

waysToLose.title: Explosive passes behind the coverage
waysToLose.body: Seattle doesn't need a great offense to beat this secondary, only a couple of shots that connect. Arizona allows explosive passes at one of the league's highest rates. Seattle's pass EPA is merely middling, but that is plenty against this defense.

waysToLose.title: Hidden yards on special teams
waysToLose.body: Seattle's special teams rank third in EPA and Arizona's rank 26th. In a game the Cardinals need to keep low-scoring and close, a few kicks of field-position swing could decide it.

nextGame.watch: Whether Arizona's line, without Gaines and possibly Williams, can give Brissett enough time to work McBride underneath. That question decides whether this looks like Week 2 again.

restOfSeason.body:
Very little in Arizona's profile looks like luck. The turnover margin is even, one-score games are split and the record tracks the point differential, so there isn't much regression coming in either direction. What should change is the schedule. After Seattle, the Rams and Kansas City, the Cardinals get a run of Washington, Philadelphia, the Jets and New Orleans, all with losing records, and Philadelphia's offense and defense rank near the bottom. The run defense and ball-control approach travel well against those teams. The secondary will keep giving up points to anyone with a capable passing game.

The offense depends on health. With Bourne gone and Wilson playing hurt, expect McBride's role to grow and the passing game to get more predictable. Brissett is steady but not explosive. A realistic finish is in the mid-single digits in wins, an improvement on last year's three and a fair first-year outcome for a staff still building.
swingFactors: Whether the pass defense stops giving up explosives
Results in the soft mid-December stretch

confidence.note: Eight games of a first-year staff, the record fits the underlying numbers, and a thinning skill group adds uncertainty.
